title: The work behind your comfort
meaning: Your home needs care shared according to your actual capacity, or familiar routines become a source of accounting and resentment.
text: A lived-in home rests on repeated actions: buying essentials, preparing food and noticing when clean towels are running out. The Empress in the physical position of Muladhara describes this practical, sustaining care. The Hierophant in energy tests your footing through an accepted model: certain things must be done simply because that is what a household should do. Justice in emotions responds to the balance of effort. You both need to feel that comfort comes from fair arrangements, rather than from someone’s unnoticed obligation to provide it.

For example, you are expecting guests and prepare several dishes as usual, although you have both had a busy week. Reducing the menu feels awkward: proper hospitality seems obliged to look this way. **A household rule costs the work it asks of you both.** Behind the attractive table are shopping, cooking and clearing up. Recognising these efforts makes it possible to discuss the custom itself while preserving enjoyment of the visit and respect for each person’s time.

Things become difficult if questioning the workload is heard as rejecting family values. Instead of changing the routine, you begin counting who did what, who gave way more often and whose tiredness matters more. The wish for fairness turns home into a place of dispute, with care offered as evidence of being right. Fair participation needs room to reconsider a familiar requirement without dismissing work already done.
